theme.name: Lower NICs for the self-employed
theme.claim: Self-employed people pay lower NICs than employees (9% vs 12% Class 4/Class 1, plus no employer NICs), so the same earnings generate materially less tax and NICs depending on employment status.

text.line: The self-employed pay the same rates of income tax as employees: 20% at the basic rate; 40% at the higher rate; and 45% at the additional rate.
Both employees and the self-employed benefit from the personal allowance, which will increase to £11,500 in April 2017.
1.6 There are some differences in the way that employed and self-employed tax is calculated.
For example, expenses not subject to income tax are typically more generous for the self-employed than the employed.
In addition, there is a losses regime in place for the self-employed, which allows them to offset losses made in one year against their income tax liability over time.

1.7 The self-employed also pay a lower rate of NICs than employees, at 9% between the lower profits limit (£8,060 in 2016-17) and the upper profits limit (£43,000 in 2016-17) compared to 12% for an employee on earnings between the same thresholds.
Currently, the self-employed also pay Class 2 NICs at a flat rate of £2.80 per week (or £145.60 a year) although this is due to be abolished from April 2018.
1.8 In addition, employer NICs adds a 13.8% charge on employees’ earnings above £8,112.

The employer is liable for paying employer NICs, but the cost of this tends to be passed on to the employee through reduced wages. No such charge is due for those engaged by a business on a self-employed basis. ** (Reference: 1)
1.9 The tax and NICs paid by an individual differs depending on whether they are employed or self-employed.

For example in 2016-17, an individual in employment with a salary of £32,000 will pay £7,073 in tax and employee NICs, whereas a self-employed person earning the same amount will pay £6,500; a difference of £573.
In addition, the employed person’s employer will have to pay an additional £3,297 in employer NICs, making a total differential of £3,870.
This extra employer NICs charge may lower the headline salary offered to the employee.
Basic rate of income tax: Employee: 20%; Self-employed: 20%.
Higher rate of income tax: Employee: 40%; Self-employed: 40%.
Additional rate of income tax: Employee: 45%; Self-employed: 45%.
Class 4 NICs for self-employed: Employee: 12%; Self-employed: 9%.
Class 1 Primary NICs for employed.
Class 4 and Class 1 Primary NICs upper rate (paid above £43,000): Employee: 2%; Self-employed: 2%.
Class 2 NICs (profits above £5,965 until 2018): Employee: -; Self-employed: £2.80pw.
Employer NICs (paid by the employer): Employee: 13.8%; Self-employed: -.

theme.name: Fiscal cost and growing self-employment
theme.claim: The foregone NICs cost the public finances an estimated £5.1 billion in 2016-17, and with self-employment rising as a share of the workforce and the planned Class 2 abolition widening the gap, this poses significant fiscal challenges.

text.line: The number of self- employed working in the UK has increased over recent decades and now accounts for 15.1% of the UK workforce.

1.18 While the difference between self-employed and employed individuals’ access to contributory benefits has diminished significantly with the introduction of the new State Pension, the abolition of Class 2 NICs from 2018 means that the difference in NICs paid was due to widen.

At the same time, the proportion of the workforce who are self-employed has risen considerably since the late 1970s, with recent growth continuing a steady upwards trend that began in the early 2000s.
This poses significant fiscal challenges.
The foregone NICs from lower rates paid by the self- employed compared with employees is estimated to cost the public finances £5.1 billion in 2016-17. ** (Reference: 5)

And the Office for Budget Responsibility have revised their self-employment forecast at Spring Budget 2017 to reflect the changing make-up of the labour market, which reduces projected tax receipts by around £1 billion a year by 2020-21.
On its own this would increase the differential between the rates of National Insurance paid by employees and those paid by the self-employed.

theme.name: Narrowed benefit access gap
theme.claim: The historical justification for lower self-employed contributions, less state support, has weakened because the new State Pension gives the self-employed the same entitlement as employees, leaving only minor differences in parental benefits and contribution-based JSA.

text.line: 1.11 NICs have a specific purpose: receipts from NICs are spent on the NHS and contributory benefits (including the State Pension).
A proportion of NICs, around 20%, goes directly to fund the NHS.
A fund separate from general taxation called the National Insurance Fund takes in NICs receipts and uses them to fund contributory benefits.
1.12 Individuals in work between the age of 16 and State Pension age pay NICs above a certain earnings or profits threshold; this provides eligibility to certain benefits.

1.13 Historically, the differences in rates of contributions reflected the fact that the self- employed received less support than employees from the state in the form of contributory welfare benefits and statutory payments, particularly the State Pension.

1.18 While the difference between self-employed and employed individuals’ access to contributory benefits has diminished significantly with the introduction of the new State Pension, the abolition of Class 2 NICs from 2018 means that the difference in NICs paid was due to widen.
Since April 2016, the self-employed also have access to the same State Pension as employees, worth £1,800 a year more to a self-employed individual than under the previous system. ** (Reference: 35)
